Separable equations

DEFINITION 1. An equation of the form

                             X1(x)Y1(y) + X2(x)Y2(y)y ′(x) = 0.                              (1)

is called an equation with variables separable or simply a separable equation.

We can rewrite DE (1) in the differential form

                             X1(x)Y1(y)dx + X2(x)Y2(y)dy = 0.

If Y1(y), X2(x) do not vanish, then (1) can be written as

              X1(x)                      Y2(y) dy                                         X1(x)
            +                   = 0   or                              = −Y2(y)     (dy = y ′(x)dx).             (2)              X2(x)   Y1(y) dx           X2(x)dx     Y1(y)dy

Integrating (2) by variable x, we obtain

                           Z  X1(x)     Z Y2(y)
                                       dx +       = c.                                (3)                                  X2(x)        Y1(y)dy

Both the integrals in (3) are indefinite and constants of integration have been absorbed in c.

Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 3, 2026                 3 / 43

For the Cauchy problem with initial condition y(x0) = y0 we can integrate (2) from x0 to x to obtain

                         Z x X1(x)     Z x Y2(y)                                     dx +            ′(x)dx = 0                                               x0 X2(x)          x0 Y1(y)y

or
                           Z x X1(x)     Z y Y2(y)
                                       dx +        = 0.                               (4)                                                  x0 X2(x)          y0 Y1(y)dy

A simpler procedure that also yields (3) and (4) is to consider dy/dx in (2) like a fraction. Multiplying
(2) by dx results in
                                   X1(x)                           = −Y2(y)                                        (5)                                  X2(x)dx     Y1(y)dy

which is a separated equation with the independent variable on the left-side, and the dependent variable
on the right-side. Equations (3) and (4) then results directly upon integration. Note that DE (5) we
can rewrite in the form
                                     g(y)dy = f (x)dx.

In some cases, an equation that is not initially separable can be reduced to a separable form through an
appropriate substitution. Consider a differential equation that can be written as

                                      y ′ = f (ax + by + c),

where a, b and c are constants. To solve it, we introduce the substitution

                                          z = ax + by + c.

(Alternatively, one may set z = ax + by, , since the constant c is absorbed into the function.)
Differentiating with respect to x, we obtain

                                        dz
                          = a + by ′.
                                       dx
Substituting y ′ = f (z) into this expression gives

                                       dz
                          = a + bf (z).
                                      dx

This equation is now separable. Indeed, assuming a + bf (z) ̸= 0, we can rewrite it as

                                          dz
                             = dx,
                                      a + bf (z)

Model with separable equation. Population growth.

Let P(t) be the size of a population at time t, and let β(t) and δ(t) be, respectively, the birth and
death rates (that is, measured per unit of population per unit time) within the population. We suppose
that β(t) and δ(t) are continuous functions. For a very short interval of time ∆t, we may assume that
β and δ are constants, so we approximate the change ∆P in the population during that interval by

                        ∆P ≈(β −δ)P∆t,

Homogeneous equations


DEFINITION 2.
Let D be a domain in R2. A function f  : D →R is called homogeneous of degree m ∈R in D  if

                 f (tx, ty) = tmf (x, y) for any x, y  such that  (x, y) ∈D, (tx, ty) ∈D, t ∈R.

EXAMPLE
The function F given by F(x, y) = x3y −x2y 2 is homogeneous of degree 4 in R2, since

                  F(tx, ty) = (tx)3ty −(tx)2(ty)2 = t4(x3y −x2y 2) = t4F(x, y).

 DEFINITION 3.
Differential equation
                                 P(x, y)dx + Q(x, y)dy = 0                                   (9)

in which P, Q are homogeneous functions of the same degree m in D, is called homogeneous in D.





Alexander Gladkov, Professor  (Belarusian State University)                 DIFFERENTIAL EQUATIONS                                  September 3, 2026                19 / 43

By using the change of function
                                            y = zx

we obtain
                               P(x, zx)dx + Q(x, zx)d(zx) = 0.

Now we use the definition of homogeneous function with t = x to get

                         xmP(1, z)dx + xmQ(1, z)(zdx + xdz) = 0.

Dividing last DE by xm, we have

                           P(1, z)dx + Q(1, z)zdx + Q(1, z)xdz = 0.

After simple transformation we obtain

                             (P(1, z) + zQ(1; z))dx + xQ(1, z)dz = 0.

Hence the DE (9) becomes DE with separable variables. Separating variables, we obtain a separated
equation with the dependent variable z on the left-side, and the independent variable x on the right-side.

                                    Q(1, z)dz                                = −dx .

                        P(tx, ty) = tmP(x, y),     Q(tx, ty) = tmQ(x, y).

Our goal is to show that under this homogeneity assumption, the differential equation (11) can always
be rewritten in the form (10).
